title: Nutrition
tagline: Classes of food, balanced diet, deficiency diseases, tooth structure and the human digestive system in outline.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Nutrition is the process by which organisms take in and use food. In human beings, food is not just a single substance but a mixture of different classes of food, each with a different job. This chapter studies the classes of food and their functions, the idea of a balanced diet and the results of deficiency, the structure of a tooth as an example of how the body is adapted to what it eats, and the outline of the human digestive system, which prepares food so that it can be used by the body.

learn.title: Classes of food and their functions

blocks.text: Human food contains several classes of nutrients, each with a different role. Carbohydrates are the main source of energy and are found in starchy foods and sugars. Proteins are needed for growth and repair and are made of amino acids. Fats provide energy and insulation and help the body absorb some vitamins. Vitamins are needed in small amounts for many body processes and help prevent deficiency diseases. Minerals are needed for making bones and teeth and for other body functions. Water is needed for all body processes and makes up a large part of the body. Roughage, or fibre, is the part of food that is not digested but helps the bowels work properly.

items.text: Rice, bread and potatoes are carbohydrate-rich foods.
items.note: Carbohydrates are the main energy foods in many diets.

items.text: Eggs, pulses and meat provide protein.
items.note: Proteins are important for growing children and for repair.

items.text: Milk, butter and cooking oil contain fats.
items.note: Fats are a concentrated source of energy.

blocks.text: A balanced diet is one that contains the right kinds and amounts of food to meet the body's needs. It should have enough carbohydrate for energy, enough protein for growth and repair, enough fat for energy and insulation, enough vitamins and minerals for proper body function, enough water, and enough roughage. If any of these is missing, deficiency diseases can develop. For example, lack of vitamin A can cause poor night vision, lack of vitamin C can cause scurvy, and lack of vitamin D can cause rickets. Lack of protein can affect growth and repair, and lack of iron can cause anaemia. So nutrition is not just about eating enough food; it is about eating the right food.

items.text: A child who lacks vitamin A may have poor night vision.
items.note: This is one of the classic deficiency examples in school biology.

items.text: Scurvy was a serious problem among sailors before fresh food was available.
items.note: Scurvy is a well-known deficiency disease caused by lack of vitamin C.

blocks.text: A tooth is adapted for biting and chewing, which are the first steps in digestion. A typical tooth has a crown, the part above the gum, and a root, the part fixed in the jaw. The crown is covered by enamel, which is the hardest substance in the body and protects the tooth. Inside the enamel is dentine, a hard tissue softer than enamel. In the centre is the pulp, which contains nerves and blood vessels. The tooth is fixed in the jaw by the periodontal fibres and bone. Different kinds of teeth have different shapes for cutting, tearing and grinding food. If food and bacteria are not cleaned away, the enamel and dentine can be damaged and decay can reach the pulp, causing pain.

items.text: Incisors are used for cutting, canines for tearing and molars for grinding.
items.note: The shape of the tooth matches its job.

items.text: A tooth with decay may become painful when the pulp is affected.
items.note: Decay reaches the pulp only after enamel and dentine have been damaged.

blocks.text: The human digestive system is a long tube called the alimentary canal, with special organs attached. Food enters through the mouth, where teeth cut and grind it and saliva from the salivary glands begins starch digestion and makes the food into a soft mass. The food then passes down the oesophagus into the stomach, where gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid and enzymes helps digestion and kills some germs. From the stomach, food enters the small intestine, where digestion continues and absorption takes place through many villi. The liver produces bile, and the pancreas produces digestive enzymes and a hormone; both are important in digestion. The large intestine absorbs water and forms faeces, which are removed from the body through the anus. The whole system is about taking in food, breaking it down, absorbing what is useful and removing what is not.

assessment.title: Nutrition: check your understanding
instructions: Answer the short questions in one or two sentences each.
For the long and analytical questions, write in full sentences and name the food classes, deficiency diseases, parts or organs clearly.
All questions are original practice; they are not past paper questions.

exercises.answer: The classes of food are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage.
exercises.explanation: All seven classes should be named.

exercises.answer: A balanced diet is one that contains the right kinds and amounts of food to meet the body's needs.
exercises.explanation: The definition should mention the right kinds and amounts of food.

exercises.answer: Protein is needed for growth and repair of the body.
exercises.explanation: The function of protein is growth and repair.

exercises.prompt: Name a deficiency disease caused by lack of vitamin D.
exercises.answer: Rickets is a deficiency disease caused by lack of vitamin D or calcium.
exercises.explanation: Rickets is the standard deficiency disease linked to vitamin D in ICSE work.

exercises.prompt: Describe the structure of a tooth.
exercises.answer: A tooth has a crown above the gum and a root fixed in the jaw. The crown is covered by enamel, the hardest substance in the body. Under the enamel is dentine, a hard tissue. In the centre is the pulp, which contains nerves and blood vessels. The tooth is fixed in the jaw by fibres and bone.
exercises.explanation: A good answer names crown, enamel, dentine and pulp and their arrangement.

exercises.answer: Food enters the mouth, where teeth cut and grind it and saliva begins starch digestion. It passes down the oesophagus into the stomach, where it is churned with gastric juice. It then enters the small intestine, where most digestion and absorption occur, helped by bile from the liver and enzymes from the pancreas. Villi absorb the products. The large intestine absorbs water and forms faeces, which leave through the anus.
exercises.explanation: A good outline should include mouth, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and the role of absorption.

questions.prompt: Which nutrient gives the main source of energy?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are the main source of energy in the diet.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing protein — that is mainly for growth and repair.

questions.prompt: Which nutrient is needed for growth and repair?
questions.explanation: Protein is needed for growth and repair of the body.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing fat — that mainly gives energy and insulation.

questions.prompt: Which is the hardest substance in the body?
questions.explanation: Enamel is the hardest substance in the body and covers the crown of the tooth.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing dentine — that is hard but softer than enamel.

questions.prompt: Which deficiency disease is caused by lack of vitamin C?
questions.explanation: Scurvy is caused by lack of vitamin C.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing rickets — that is linked to vitamin D or calcium.

questions.prompt: Which part of the digestive system absorbs most nutrients?
questions.explanation: Most digestion and absorption occur in the small intestine.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the large intestine — that mainly absorbs water.

questions.explanation: The liver produces bile, which helps digestion.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing pancreas — that produces digestive enzymes and hormones.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: food rich in fibre that is not digested is called ________.
questions.explanation: Roughage is the indigestible fibre that helps the bowels work properly.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'vitamin' — that is not the fibre term.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blanks: the soft centre of a tooth containing nerves and blood vessels is the ________.
questions.explanation: The pulp is the soft centre of the tooth containing nerves and blood vessels.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'enamel' — that is the hard outer covering, not the centre.

questions.prompt: State three classes of food and one function of each.
questions.answer: Carbohydrates give energy; proteins help growth and repair; fats give energy and insulation. Other correct classes with their functions are also acceptable.
questions.explanation: Any three classes with their functions carry the marks.
questions.commonMistake: Giving three classes but no functions, or wrong functions.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a tooth.
questions.answer: A tooth has a crown above the gum and a root fixed in the jaw. The crown is covered by enamel, which is the hardest part. Under the enamel is dentine. In the centre is the pulp, which contains nerves and blood vessels. The tooth is fixed in the jaw by fibres and bone.
questions.explanation: A good answer names crown, enamel, dentine and pulp and their arrangement.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the pulp is the hardest part — it is the soft centre.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a balanced diet and why deficiency diseases occur.
questions.answer: A balanced diet is one that contains the right kinds and amounts of food to meet the body's needs for energy, growth, repair and proper body function. It should include carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage. Deficiency diseases occur when a nutrient is missing or not enough in the diet. For example, lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, lack of vitamin D can cause rickets, and lack of iron can cause anaemia. So deficiency diseases are due to lack of a particular nutrient, not just to eating too little food overall.
questions.explanation: A full answer should define balanced diet and explain that deficiency diseases come from lack of a nutrient, with an example.
questions.commonMistake: Saying deficiency diseases happen only when a person eats too little food — the cause is lack of a nutrient.

questions.prompt: A child has poor night vision and is not eating many green vegetables or milk. Which nutrient may be lacking? Explain.
questions.answer: The child may be lacking vitamin A. Vitamin A is needed for healthy eyes, and deficiency can cause poor night vision. Milk and green vegetables are sources of vitamin A, so a diet lacking them may lead to deficiency. This fits the symptom because night blindness is a classic vitamin A deficiency sign.
questions.explanation: The answer should name vitamin A, the symptom it affects and the likely cause from the diet described.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the lack is of vitamin D — that mainly affects bones, not night vision.
